_podcast.theme_description: Today we explore how Cariboo and BC Indigenous nations are using technology on their own terms — for language revitalization, land stewardship, cultural preservation, and self-determined governance. We're looking for stories that centre Indigenous voices and leadership in innovation, where technology serves community sovereignty rather than replacing it.
_podcast.theme_scoring_prompt:
Rate how well this article fits the theme 'Indigenous Lands & Innovation' — Indigenous nations using technology, governance, and stewardship on their own terms.

OUT OF SCOPE — score 0-9: geopolitical and war news with no Indigenous rights angle; general wildfire and wildlife-service updates not led by or directly affecting Indigenous communities or guardians; provincial forestry and environmental policy with no explicit First Nations involvement; consumer tech and gadget reviews; science with no Indigenous stewardship or sovereignty context; crime and judicial news unrelated to Indigenous rights.

CALIBRATION — apply this ladder to everything else. Indigenous-led journalism on governance, rights, and self-determination is a strong fit on its own: a technology hook raises a score but is NOT required to reach the top band.
- 80-100: Excellent Indigenous-led reporting. Cariboo stories bridging governance or culture AND technology land here (Tŝilhqot'in/Secwépemc/Dakelh language revitalization tech, guardian programs using sensors and drones, GIS land mapping, Indigenous-led connectivity, digital heritage projects) — and so does outstanding national coverage of sovereignty, treaty, and land rights.
- 55-79: Solid pan-Canadian Indigenous governance, sovereignty, land rights, treaty, or reconciliation journalism — APTN, Eagle Feather News, or IndigiNews-style coverage of First Nations governance, MMIWG, land claims, self-determination, and Indigenous-led services. Most Indigenous governance journalism belongs HERE, not below.
- 30-54: Indigenous cultural, community, or human-interest stories (awards, events, ceremonies) with limited governance substance, or BC land-stewardship and environmental stories with meaningful First Nations involvement.
- 10-29: General BC land, environmental, or forestry stories that mention Indigenous communities only in passing.

ANCHORS: 'Tŝilhqot'in Nation launches drone-based caribou monitoring on title lands' → 98. 'First Nations leaders reject BC's revised land-title framework' → 75. 'Secwépemc language app reaches 1,000 learners' → 88. 'BC Wildfire Service updates evacuation alerts for the Interior' → 8.

Score 0-100 where 100 is a perfect thematic match and 0 is completely unrelated.

items.title: [Fast Company] Popular pet food recalled after 3 dogs got sick in latest U.S. salmonella scare
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

The ongoing salmonella outbreaks that have taken grip this summer have now reached dogs.

Oma’s Pride, a raw pet food brand based in Avon, Connecticut, has issued a voluntary recall on 639 bags of its Woof Complete Canine Chicken Recipe due to salmonella contamination. 

The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) said it received a consumer complaint about the product, tested it, and found it tested positive for salmonella, according to a recall notice shared on Monday, August 17. Oma’s Pride is investigating the source.

So far, there have been three reports of dogs experiencing illness, the notice states. The announcement also warns that humans could contract salmonella infections when handling the impacted foods. 

Fast Company reached out to Oma’s Pride for additional comment. The pet food brand is owned by Miller Foods.

This year has seen brands like Kroger and Utz face salmonella outbreaks, with one notable outbreak being linked to jalapeño peppers and impacting numerous retailers in states across the country.

What products are affected?

The dog food recall is limited to the Woof Complete Canine Chicken Recipe, 6 lb bag. The stand-up pouch is made up of 12 different 8-oz vacuum-sealed portions of food. Here are the identifying points to look out for:

  • Produced: January 27, 2026
  • Best by date: January 27, 2029
  • UPC: 8 7938400145 9
  • SKU: F-WOOFC-6
  • Lot number: BB012729

Where was the product sold? 

Oma’s Pride distributed the impacted Woof Complete Canine Chicken Recipe bags between February 12, 2026, and May 15, 2026. The product was sold through wholesale, retail, and online direct orders in these states:

  • Arizona
  • California
  • Indiana
  • Kentucky
  • Louisiana
  • Maryland
  • New Jersey
  • Nevada
  • New York
  • Pennsylvania
  • Virginia 

What should I do if I have this product?

Immediately stop giving your dog any impacted bag of Woof Complete Canine Chicken Recipe. Oma’s Pride warns against selling or donating the product and says to throw it out. 

“Wash and sanitize pet food bowls, cups, and storage containers,” the notice states. “Always ensure you wash and sanitize your hands after handling recalled food or any utensils that have come into contact with it.” 

You can contact Oma’s Pride directly for a refund at 1-800-678-OMAS or by emailing hello@omaspride.com. 

What salmonella symptoms should I look out for in my dog? 

According to the FDA release, pets with salmonella infections can exhibit symptoms such as: 

  • Lethargy
  • Diarrhea or bloody diarrhea
  • Fever
  • Vomiting
  • Decreased appetite
  • Abdominal pain

The announcement warns that “infected but otherwise healthy pets can be carriers and infect other animals or humans.”

Contact your veterinarian if your pet exhibits any symptoms of a salmonella infection. 

Salmonella can cause similar symptoms in humans, including abdominal pain, diarrhea, fever, nausea, and vomiting.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] Scientists discover a natural Arctic cloud factory missing from climate models
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

A newly discovered Arctic process can dramatically boost the number of particles that help form clouds. Near melting sea ice, sunlight reacts with chemicals released by the ocean, algae, and ice, causing cloud-seeding particles to multiply by as much as 50 times in a day. Because the active ice-edge region is growing as sea ice retreats, the effect could become increasingly important. Scientists now want to add the process to climate models to see how much it could reshape Arctic warming.
